utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Black will be handling the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Unless the Chamber has any initial business, I would call the next Prosecution witness, Lieutenant Colonel Jozef Poje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Main the witness please take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Can you understand me okay?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Good morning. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If at any time you can't understand one of my questions, please just tell me and I'll try to state it more clearly.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Also, if you have any trouble with the headphones, with the volume or if they're slipping, just let us know and the usher will help you. Now, can you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: I am Jozef Poje.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And I'm ask you just a few questions about your background before we get to the substance of your expert report. You were born in 1948 in Slovenia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes. I was born on the 4th of March, 1948, in Ptuj, the Republic of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And did you move with your family to Croatia at some point in your childhood?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: In 1961, I moved from Ptuj to Pula in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Please briefly tell the Trial Chamber about your experience in the JNA up until the year 1991. Please tell what positions you held and where you were based for each of those positions.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: I went to secondary school or gymnasium and graduated in 1967. In that same year, I went to the military academy in Belgrade, and I graduated from the military academy in 1971 in Zadar as an artillery second lieutenant from 1971 to 1975 I was the commander of a mortar battery, 120 millimetre, in Idovcina, and that was the 253rd infantry platoon, regiment. Then I was transferred to the anti-armour battery. I was the commander of that battery in Ptuj. In 1978, I was redeployed to the training centre in Zadar where I was a teacher in the subject of theory and the rules of shooting, marksmanship. As a teacher I worked in the educational centre of Zadar for 13 years, and at that time I taught for a year in the school for reserve officers. For ten years I was at the military academy in the artillery department, and then I spent two years as a professor in the subject of firing theory and commander of various divisions. On the 2nd of August, 1991, I decided to leave the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: From Zadar I went to Slovenia, and I gained employment in the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Slovenia. I worked -- spent one year working in the department for development and education and tuition, and from 1992 up until the present day I have been working in the educational centre which is part of the military school centre and is now called the command for the doctrine, development, education, and training of forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So are you an active member of the Slovenian armed forces?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: I am still an active member of the armed forces of the Republic of Slovenia and, as I've already said, I worked in the command for the doctrine, development, training, and education where I am head of the department for artillery in the centre for doctrinaire matters and development.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What military rank do you currently hold?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: I currently hold the rank of lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In a previous answer you mentioned that you were a teacher in the subjects of theory and the rules of shooting. Did that relate to artillery or some other kind of weapon?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: I worked in the artillery as a commander and in the school centre as well. The subject was firing theory, theory and practice, using artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Has your teaching been purely theoretical or have you engaged also in artillery exercises over the years?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: During training, in addition to theoretical teaching in the classroom we also did practical work, firing, artillery firing. And while I was in Zadar, I fired about 15.000 different projectiles ranging from 20-millimetre projectiles until the -- up until the 155-millimetre projectiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Finally on the broad subject of background information, did you testify as an expert on artillery issues in the Strugar case in this Tribunal in 2004?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: In 2004, I was here as an expert witness, that is true, to testify about artillery matters in the Strugar case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Lieutenant Colonel. Now, let me turn to this case, the Prosecutor versus Milan Martic. Were you asked by the Office of the Prosecutor to prepare an expert report in this case?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I was asked to prepare a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And did you in fact prepare such a report?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: I did. I wrote the report, and it is 80 pages long.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could have trial Exhibit number 7 on the e-court, please. Lieutenant Colonel, in just a moment on one of the screens in front of you you'll see a document. Is that the report that you prepared for this case?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes, it is. That is the report I prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And I also notice you have a document at the witness table with you. Is that this same report?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes, it is. That's the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, this report was admitted by your decision of 13 January 2006. It is trial Exhibit number 7. And what I would propose to do is give you each a hard copy of this report - the witness has hard copy - and that is simply because we'll be looking at several documents, so you can't have the report and the document on the screen at the same time. I this I it will be more convenient. If I could pass those to you. I do have another copy in B/C/S if the Defence needs one, but I think they may have their own copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And one more thing, Your Honours. We did notice in proofing a minor correction, and so I have page 33 just in the English version. It's just a translation problem. The figures in these diagrams which I've just handed up have the wrong numbers. The B/C/S was correct but we failed to make the correction in the final version of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Poje, what were you specifically asked to address in your report?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise to my learned friend for interrupting him, but might the accused have a copy of the report in his own language? He don't have one at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I do have an extra copy. I'd be happy to provide it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sorry for the interruption, Lieutenant Colonel Poje. Just a procedural thing there. My question was: What specifically were you asked to address in your expert report?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: The main task I was assigned in writing this report was to give my professional opinion about the use of the self-propelled multiple rocket launcher M87 Orkan and its effect on the city of Zagreb on the 2nd and 3rd of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just so it's clear were you asked to provide a legal opinion about the lawfulness of the shelling of Zagreb or some other kind of opinion?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: No, I wasn't asked to leave a legal opinion about its effect on Zagreb but as an artillery expert to provide information and data about the effects of Orkan as a weapon, purely technically, from the technical aspect, to provide technical data of the use of the Orkan and its effects, the effects of the Orkan multiple rocket launcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And one more question related to the scope of your report. Were you asked to analyse any activities of the Croatian armed forces?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: No. I was not asked to address the activities of the Croatian armed forces, so that in my report I make no mention of this subject matter. That is to say I don't deal with the Croatian armed forces and their activities in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What kinds of sources did you use in preparing your expert report?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: In preparing my report, I used existing military literature, that is to say the existing literature used by the Yugoslav People's Army. Secondly, I used reports and documents provided to me by the Prosecution for the purposes of writing my report. And thirdly, I used some other sources, primarily those I found on the internet sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, let me turn to the substance of your report. Your report includes a lot of relevant information, but I'm going to focus here in court just on the most important aspects. So to begin, please turn to section 3.8.1. This is on page 45 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And on page 37 in English, Your Honour. Lieutenant Colonel, here you discuss in this section the characteristics of the M87 Orkan multiple rocket launcher. Before get into those details, one quick question regarding sources. In footnote 18, you cite to a website. Did you consult any other sources regarding the characteristics of the Orkan M87?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: In my report I stated the literature in the footnotes, but I omitted to include this literature. I studied the literature, the tactics -- firing tactics for Orkan and some other sources that I also found on the internet. Anyway, I decided to leave that in the report, because the material found on that page is the most complete information set out in the greatest detail on that site. So despite the fact that I used other sources, the material I state here I compared to the firing tables with some other internet sites. So there are no vital differences with respect to the basic characteristics and intentions of Orkan, and there weren't any vital differences between that and the material I studied.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Very well. Based on all the material that you viewed, what is the Orkan M87 weapon system designed to do? What is its main use in combat?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: The self-propelled multiple rocket launcher M87 Orkan is intended to for action against live force and materiel force, and its destruction power is great. That is the main aim of the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When you say live force and materiel force, could you put that in ordinary language for us? What kind of targets is it normally used against?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: The multiple rocket launcher intended for -- is intended for fire support of the units, of the corps in the army. It can neutralise all types of force. When I say live force, I mean the units themselves that are being targeted. It can also be used against armoured vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Maybe this is -- is -- seems obvious, but when you say the units themselves, are you referring to personnel to soldiers themselves or some other aspect of the units, just so it's clear please.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: First of all, I mean the soldiers, because we know that units are made up of soldiers and technical equipment, and the Orkan was designed to act against the military unit in its entirety, both soldiers and technical equipment and materiel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Was the M87 Orkan designed to be used against densely populated areas such as a city?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: In view of the fact that it has high dispersion capabilities, Orkan is not principally suitable for use in populated areas. It is designed for use outside populated areas. The reason for this is primarily that its effects in populated areas, regardless of the fact that there might be military targets in populated areas, there is a high probability that parts of the rocket should be dispersed and affect the civilian population, especially when the civilian population has not been evacuated on time or has not taken refuge or shelter. So I would like to mention once again Orkan is not intended for deployment in populated areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: We'll come back to the subject of impact dispersion in some detail a little later. Right now, according to your report the M87 Orkan consists of a number of components including launcher vehicle, et cetera, and I'd like to ask you a number of questions about those components. So please look again at the beginning of section 3.8.1. This is on page 45 in B/C/S and page 37 in English. Lieutenant Colonel, what do we see in the photograph on that page?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Would you repeat the page, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I believe it should be on page 45. Also, you can see it on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes. I can see it. That is an example of a launcher, the M87 Orkan launcher. The vehicle plus the launcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You discussed the launcher and the vehicle in some detail in your report, but could you briefly point out the most important characteristics of the launcher and the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: As you can see on this picture, it is a vehicle with a launcher. The launcher has 12 barrels. It is a 12-barrel launcher and it is positioned, mounted on a FAP vehicle, 9-tonne, 8X8 FAP vehicle, a truck which enables great manoeuvrability, great manoeuvre capability. It has a massive 15 tonnes, and when the launcher is full, the overall mass of the launcher is about 32 tonnes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How long does it take for the Orkan M87 to prepare for a firing once it arrives at a launch location?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: The preparation time, firing preparation time, is two to three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Does the Orkan M87 launch all of its rockets at once or does it launch them simultaneously or, excuse me, one after another?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: You can effect individual launches or simultaneous in a burst of gunfire regulating the firing on two, four, or six seconds, which means from barrel to barrel, and the interval between the firing from the first to the last barrel is two seconds, four seconds -- intervals of two seconds, four seconds, and six seconds, firing intervals.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What is the approximate firing range of the M87 Orkan?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Generally speaking, in the literature that I studied it states that the maximum firing range is something above 50 kilometres. In the firing charts, numerical firing charts, this distance is given as 51.093 metres. And I'd like to mention that that is what you find in the literature and in the firing charts, the maximum distance is greater than a little greater than 50 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention now to the rocket. What kind of rocket is fired by the M87 Orkan?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Orkan can use two types of projectiles with two types of warheads and cluster charges. It is M87, 262-millimetre calendar with two warheads with a shaped charge in one warhead and a cluster charge in the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about one of the warheads in a moment, but before we get to that, is the R262-millimetre rocket a guided or an unguided weapon?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: As in all multiple rocket launchers, the Orkan is unguided. It has a classical type trajectory without guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could you perhaps explain a little bit more what it means that it's a classical type projectile with no guidance?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: That means that the projectile flies based on the elevation taken and the speed it gains when leaving the barrel. At the moment when the rocket propulsion engine ceases to work, then the flight is, as we say, a free flight. As of that moment, we can no longer correct or adjust its trajectory. It continues its flight based on the initial data given at the firing, when the calculations were made for the firing. Based on the elevation of the barrel and based on the initial speed, the projectile follows a trajectory concluding its flight at the place of target foreseen. Concerning the actual flight of the rocket, of the projectile, we cannot exercise any control over its trajectory once the initial parameters have been exhausted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. Now, let me go back to the war -- you mentioned two types of warhead and both are mentioned in your report, but could you ask you to describe briefly the cluster warhead that uses the shaped charge and fragmentation bomblets.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: We stated that Orkan has two types of warheads, the fragmentation bomblets warhead and a shaped charged projectile used for anti-armour activity. There are 288 shaped charge bomblets with 420 pellets each. The actual head opens up some 800 to 1.000 metres away from the target. The container containing the bomblets is cut with the four mounted blades, and the bomblets drop on the target. Each bomblet has a stabiliser regulating the flight of the bomblet. At the same time, this textile band alarms or arms the mechanical fuse when there is the contact with the ground. Bomblets have a shaped charge with fragmentation effect which is achieved by some 420 pellets inside each bomblet. Its destruction force covers the perimeter of some 10 metres. It also has a fragmentation effect, because the explosive charge in the bomblet is constructed in such a way that a fragmentation cone is created piercing armour, i.e., steel up to 60-millimetres thick, which makes it able to pierce any existing type of armour or tank from above.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. When you say that the destructive force covers a perimeter of some 10 metres, is that for each of the 288 bomblets that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes. If we take one bomblet containing 420 pellets and in one container in the warhead we have 288 bomblets, meaning the overall amount is 288 times 420 pellets. The effect of the pellets of a specific bomblet is 10 metres. Therefore, each bomblet can cover around 10 metres with its pellets. Some sources mention the figure of more than 10 metres, but 10 metres is the mean value of the destruction force of the pellets of each bomblet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And how large of an area do these bomblets, the 288 bomblets from one rocket, cover?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: The area covered by the 288 bomblets is around two hectares.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: With the assistance of the court officer, I'd now like to show you an illustration which is 65 ter Exhibit number 21. If that could be brought up on our screens, please. Lieutenant Colonel, if you can look at this. Perhaps we can make it smaller. That's fine. The full-page view is fine. Lieutenant Colonel, could you describe what's shown in this illustration on the screen in front of you, please?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: We can see on this illustration that -- the place of launching or the place of deployment of the launcher is. We can see the trajectory of the projectile, the point where the fragmentation charge is opened up and the fall of the bomblets. In the end, there is an ellipsis affected by the pellets. That area and the ellipsis shown, according to the references I used, amounts to some two hectares. That is the area where the 288 bomblets fall from each fragmentation charge of the warhead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could this document be given an exhibit number and admitted into evidence, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Exhibit will be 771.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could see the next document which is actually a group of photos bearing the earned 06004077, please. Lieutenant Colonel, could you please tell us what's shown on these photographs on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: The three photographs on the screen show a bomblet from the fragmentation warhead of the Orkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And is this the kind of bomblet that you've just been describing?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes. Those are the bomblets I had previously described. We see the body of the bomblets, and we can see -- we can make out the pellets. We see two bands used to stabilise the flight and to arm the fuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Perhaps with the assistance of the usher I'd like to ask you to mark on this photograph the things that you've just mentioned. First, Lieutenant Colonel, if you could just draw an arrow to one of the textile bands that you mentioned that stabilises the flight. Draw an arrow to those and put a number 1 next to it, please.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: This is the band.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. And you also mentioned that you can see the pellets. Could you draw an arrow to one of places where you can see the pellets and put a number 2 next to that, please.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, can we please tender this marked version of the photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we do what?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Tender this marked version into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The marked version of that photograph is tendered into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number. Can I just ask a question, Mr. Black. That number 2, you asked the witness to show us the pellets, and the witness points to a single rounded cylinder object. I'm not seeing pellets, I'm seeing one object.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it will become clear in just a moment. The following exhibit, I hope, will make that clear, and if not, I'll return to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit 772.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'd forgotten about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Actually, I notice that the witness has made some additional markings to try and clarify this. If we could perhaps sorry to save this and make it the following exhibit, perhaps. Thank you very much. Could that receive the next exhibit number, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The next picture is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 773, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And just for the record I guess I should say the witness drew another arrow to the pellets and again put the number 2 next to it. At this point if I could show the witness 65 ter number 13, which is actually -- it's not a document. It's one of the deactivated bomblets from the Orkan. It's been deactivated, Your Honours. There's no danger. Perhaps, actually -- maybe we should show this briefly to Defence counsel. I don't know if they've had a chance to examine this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no need. Thank you. No need, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Poje, what is it that you have in your hands now?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: I have a bomblet in my hand coming from the fragmentation or a cluster charge of the Orkan warhead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And can you -- can you show us the textile band that you referred to and give us an idea of how that operates, please?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: The bomblet drops approximately in this position as I am holding it now. This band stabilises the bomblet to keep it from swerving left and right. It makes it possible for the bomblet to drop in a straightforward manner to the ground. At the same time, it arms the fuse of the bomblet, making it possible for the bomblet to explode upon impacting the ground. When that explosion occurs, the pellets are released. We can see them here. There's also a cone affecting the object in the way of the bomblet. As I said, it is able to pierce a steel surface up to 60 millimetres thick. When it explodes, the pellets we can see here impact personnel. I have in mind the soldiers. And a successful impact of such a bomblet would cover approximately 10 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Lieutenant Colonel. If we could perhaps hand the bomblet up to the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think Your Honours could then see quite easily the pellets and understand a little bit about how the bomblet is put together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I think we don't really understand this function of the pellets. Can you explain to us --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel, could you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: -- where are the pellets and how would they explode, in which direction, how they will be released and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Poje, in response to Judge Hoepfel's question, could you give us an explanation about how the pellets on the bomblet -- how they're released and how they have an impact on personnel?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: This is an unexploded bomblet. References mention that around 10 per cent of bomblets go unexploded. This was such an example. As you can see the very bomblet, there is a cylinder in which you can see the pellets. When the explosion occurs, meaning when the bomblet impacts on a surface, this is an explosion dispersing the pellets all around on a more or less horizontal plane. And those pellets are used against personnel, against soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we're not seeing the pellets. Where are the pellets, or are you saying generally the pellets would be contained in this part? This is one that has been used already. Or is it an unused one? We're not really -- I am not seeing the pellets that you keep speaking about, as you can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if it's a vocabulary problem, but maybe I can ask the once one question quickly. Lieutenant Colonel Poje, we've been using the word pellets in English. Does that refer essentially to very small metal balls? Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes, these are small balls, and we can see that given their size their dispersion and the area they cover is relatively small, covering an area of around 10 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I understand the principle. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm slow on the uptake.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Not at all, Your Honour. I want this to be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see little small ball held onto the cylinder by some plastic tape. Are those what we refer -- and there are three of them that I see, or four -- yes, three that I see. Is that what you mean by pellets, or also on the body of the cylinder I see lots of dots right around it, the circumference of the cylinder. Are those the pellets that then explode and scatter around?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps if it could be passed back to the witness for him to answer your question. By way of explanation. This was used as an exhibit in the Rule 61 proceedings in this case back in 1996, I believe, and that's why three of the pellets are essentially taped onto the bomblet. That's something that was done by way of explanation in those proceedings, I believe. But hopefully --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Poje, can you answer the Judge's question, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Bearing in mind we know nothing about military.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The pellets on the outside, the little balls taped, are used by way of illustration to show what those balls really look like. Such balls or pellets are inside the cylinder originally. When the bomblets impacts, there is an explosion, and those pellets inside the cylinder fly all around impacting personnel immediately close to the bomblets covering the area of about 10 metres. Those pellets are inside the body of the cylinder, and if we were to count them, we would be supposed to come up with a total of 240. At the same time, there is the cluster cylinder at the end of it which pierces armour as opposed to the pellets that affect personnel. I hope I was clear enough, because I don't know any other way to explain it. I tried to be as simple as I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: May I ask you additionally, first, you mentioned the number 240. Is that -- should that be 420 exactly, because first you -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me clarify. In the report there is the figure of 240, but I mixed up the digits. We can verify that against the firing tables to see what the actual number is. I believe the exact number is -- and the correct number is 420 pellets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. This is the number you used before also. And the surface of the cylinder which shows these several points is not consisting of the pellets. The pellets would be inside the cylinder; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are the pellets, those you can see, inside the cylinder. The pellets or the balls are inside the cylinder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks. Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: One last question on this, Lieutenant Colonel Poje, before you put it down. Are the small balls or are the pellets covered by a transparent coating on this example, this unexploded bomblet?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So what -- what looks like points underneath that plastic are actually more examples of the metal balls. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Unless the Trial Chamber has further questions, I would ask that this be made an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Black, this is what my question was about, what you just discussed now. It seems to me that it wouldn't then be a very exact description to say the pellets will be inside the cylinder. So it would be more appropriate to say they are around the cylinder or -- and then how would they be fixed on the outside of the cylinder if not -- or is this plastic band, is that the usual thing and the tape holding these three extra pellets is now put after that additionally on the thing? Yes? Is that right? Can we say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These three were taped on, but the pellets are actually welded onto the bomblet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm trying to get the part of the transcript where my question lies. Without finding it, let me see if I can remember what the witness said. The witness said that these are pellets that injure personnel, and then I think I understood him to say there is also a -- just a cylinder at the end which pierces armoured vehicles or steel. Is it at the end of the open-ended side of the cylinder, and is that portion of the bomblet on this exhibit or is it not there?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Poje, could you please explain how a projectile like this can pierce armour? How does that work?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: In this bomblet we have an explosive charge, usually trotyl. The shape of the charge is the shape of a funnel, is in the shape of a funnel. When an explosion takes place, on impact, when the bomblet impacts the obstacle, the explosive charge is activated, and due to the shape of the charge a cumulative beam or spray is created with its focus on the obstacle and target itself. The force of this cumulative beam or spray is so great because it is concentrated, because it is the shape of a funnel. It is so concentrated the point of concentration at the obstacle that enables the beam to pierce the armour or steel up to 60 millimetres. That means -- well, it's quite simple. Let me demonstrate this. When this bomblet touches the obstacle an explosion takes place. The little pellets disperse in a circle all around and, for the most part, affect personnel, the live force, although their lethal power is not strong, but the cumulative beam that is created pierces the armour, pierces a steel sheet, for example. If you look inside, you'll see the shape that this has. And because of that shape, on the surface of the obstacle it is a point of contact which we call the focus, which is where the entire force of the explosive charge is concentrated into that one point, and that force enables piercing to take place, the piercing of the armour, steel, or what have you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm satisfied.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could this now be made an exhibit and given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The bomblet, am I right? Is that called a bomblet?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The bomblet is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That will be Exhibit 774.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And if we could see one more document at this point. It's 65 ter number 2276. And if this could be brought on e-court and shown page 5 to begin with, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Poje, what does this document purport to be based on this page that you see before you now?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: This document contains parts of the Orkan rocket which were found in Zagreb. That is to say it contains photographs of parts of the rocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And if I could just show you a couple of particular pages, the first one I believe is identified by ERN in e-court and so it's 00312114. If we could see that page, please. Lieutenant Colonel Poje, what's shown in these two photographs?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: These two photographs show parts of the rocket. On the upper picture, number 1, you can even see the markings of the rocket, the specifications. It is 262-millimetre M87, which tells you that that is the rocket in question. So they are data about the rocket. The second photograph, number 2, is once again a portion, a part of the rocket itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could move two pages ahead, please, to 00312116. Lieutenant Colonel Poje, it's somewhat small, but could you tell if these are photographs of the type of bomb that we've just looked at?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes. Those are the bomblets that we held in our hands a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just understand. These are pictures of exhibits found on the ground in Zagreb? Is that what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's what the document says, Your Honour. I don't know whether this witness has any knowledge about that, but perhaps a subsequent witness will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Sorry, is it of the type or the actual bomblets themselves that fell?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know. I don't believe this witness can respond to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could this document be made an exhibit, please, and receive a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This one has on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What about the previous ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: They're just different pages of the same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Thank you very much. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 775, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Poje, I won't spend much time on the remaining two components, the M87 Orkan which you describe in your report, namely the firing -- fire control system and the transport reloading vehicle, but just very briefly can the M87 Orkan weapon system take into account meteorological conditions at the time that its fired?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: In order to determine the initial firing elements, the Orkan system has a separate computer by which that is possible. The initial elements for firing are determined, in principle, with the help of a computer that the Orkan system has, on the basis of coordinates of the fire positions and targets. Secondly, on the basis of exact ballistic conditions of firing. And thirdly, on the basis of exact meteorological data and information. The coordinates of the fire positions and the target positions are determined in one of the ways of topographic, geographical preparation charts. Ballistic data is collected on the fire position by measurement but also from documentation. Meteorological information, in principle, is received from the meteorological station as a weather bulletin or meteorological bulletin. All this data and information are entered into the computer of the Orkan system, and according to an algorithm, a special algorithm, it is able to calculate the initial elements, the input elements. The azimuth, the range, the elevation, the timing of the fuse, all that is calculated, and those are the basic elements that are then adjusted on the artillery piece or rocket, and it is with this basic information that you launch your rocket at the target selected.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a couple more questions about this section of your report. At the end of the section you provide a table of tactical and technical characteristics of the M87 Orkan. Are the -- are the figures given in this table, are they precise figures, are they approximations, or are they a combination of both?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At what page are we.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's page 46 of the English version. And page 55 of the B/C/S version, I believe.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the end of that description for the Orkan technical characteristics or, rather, the tactical technical characteristics for Orkan shown in the table on page 46 are ones that are approximate, mean ones. And we have other documents which show us the exact figures. These are figures of principle. So in this table or chart we see that the range, for example, is 5 to 50 kilometres. In the firing tables and charts, we can see that the maximum distance is greater than 50 kilometres. So it doesn't tell us exactly how big the distance is, but it says 50 -- about 50 kilometres. The numerical tables give us a maximum range, recorded range, of 51.093 metres. So that table just gives us the principles and average figures for the Arkan system. Although some of the figures there are 100 per cent correct, others might not be 100 per cent correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me ask you specifically about the figures for dispersion and range and dispersion in line for the maximum range. Are those precise values or approximate values?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Those values, the figures mentioned here as dispersion in range for the maximum range, for example, or dispersion in line for the maximum range, Vd and Vp are -- the abbreviations are given -- approximate values are given in that table, and they allow us at a glance to see what the dispersion will be, whereas exact data for every range and distance is found in the firing table. You can read them in the firing table. So this table just provides you with global figures and the principle, not precision for a specific range, because the only of this table is not to provide exact and precise figures for the Vd and Vp or dispersion in range and dispersion in line, but in principle what those figures should be. Now, if you're interested in what this would be, for example, 47.200 metres, then you would take up your firing table, look at columns 11 and 12, and would you able to read the values used there, the dispersion figures based on individual Vd and Vp ellipses of dispersion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just one more question and then we'll have to it take our usual break. When doing the calculations in your report, did you use the values at this table here at the end of 3.8.1 or did you use the values from the firing tables that you've just discussed?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: All the calculations that I used in order to give you a picture of the dispersion I used firing tables to do that. So not this table here. Not the tactical technical characteristics table, but the firing table figures. Except for column 1, which gives you the distance, the range -- or, rather, the distance and range were used, and then columns 11 and 12 which show you the individual ellipses for the Vd and Vp values or dispersion in range for the maximum range and the dispersion in line for the maximum range.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When we come back from the break we'll get into that detail?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this is a convenient time for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Black. We're going to take a short break the we'll come back at quarter to eleven. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Poje, I'm going to turn now to a new section -- a different section of your report. It's section 6.2. And that appears on page 64 of the English and I believe page 76 in the B/C/S, or perhaps 75. And my first question for you is: What is impact dispersion? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Impact dispersion belongs to the group of accidental errors. If we fire two projectiles under roughly the same conditions, or we think they are roughly the same conditions, those two same projectiles do not follow the same trajectory. They follow two different trajectories, which means that we're going to get two hits. Now, due to the different conditions, when the projectiles are fired all the projectiles will have their own paths, their own trajectories, and that means what we mean when we say impact dispersion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And how is the impact dispersion of a particular artillery weapon fired at a particular distance, how is that determined or calculated?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: As I've already said, because of the different firing conditions there is dispersion that occurs. Now, if we take the centre of the dispersion pattern, in theory dispersion is an endless circle, but the dispersion image is actually smaller. It is not infinite, and it is plus/minus 4 Vd, and plus/minus Vd -- Vp. Dispersion in range line for the maximum range a dispersion in line for the maximum range [as interpreted]. And these are semi-axes of dispersion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me ask a just a number of questions?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me ask you just a couple of questions. You mention a formula which also appears in your report. It's on page 65 in English. On what theory is this formula based? How is this formula derived?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: If we fire a large quantity of projectiles from a barrel, we will have a beam of trajectories. If that beam of trajectories is cut across with a vertical plane, we get a dispersion pattern which is in the shape of an ellipsis. It's elliptic. Now, the end points on a horizontal plane of that ellipsis we will get the pattern of impact, which is also an ellipse. This elliptical dispersion moves within the ranges from the mean target left and right, plus/minus 4, deviation plus/minus Vd, and plus/minus 4 Vp. And plus/minus range and distance Vd and Vp. That is the ellipse in which we say all the projectiles fired from the barrel will fall, within that range.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you just right there. Before I ask you to go through the specifics and show us these calculations, this formula and the ellipse that you've just described, is that -- is that based on mathematics? Is that based on an experiment? What is the basis of that? How do you arrive at this formula that you've described?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: The pattern of dispersion can be arrived at analytically with the help of a ballistic model or on the basis of firing experiments. Today, the analytical, practical way is used of arriving at the pattern of dispersion. The size of the dispersion with respect to direction and distance are Vd and Vp, and that is found in the firing tables. So you can read your firing tables and revert to the firing tables wherever you need them. And on the basis of those amounts and figures, we are able to determine the overall pattern of dispersion. The firing tables contain semi-axes, that is to say Vp and Vd for dispersion patterns. In order to obtain the overall pattern of dispersion and on the basis of probability and Gauss's law, the overall pattern of dispersion is composed of or is plus/minus 4 Vp times plus/minus 4 Vd, which means that the axes of the dispersion pattern are equal to 8 Vp times 8 Vd.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that explanation. I'm going to get to that in just a moment. Let me ask you one more question about what you said. You talked about firing tables. Do firing tables exist for all artillery weapons? It's not necessary that you get anything out. I think I'll be able to show you what you need.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Every artillery piece has its own firing table or tables, and every weapon has its own characteristics. So the firing tables for a 105-millimetre howitzer will not correspond to the conditions of firing for a 155 howitzer. So you have separate firing tables for each individual weapon or artillery piece.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'd like to show you on the screen, with the assistant of the court officer and the usher, 65 ter Exhibit number 2275. If we could bring that up, please. And I think the first page we need to look at is page 19 in e-court. Lieutenant Colonel Poje, what is this document that we're seeing now on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: The document that is on the screen is the first page of the firing table for multiple rocket systems, 262-millimetre M87 Orkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And are these in fact the firing tables that you used in preparing your report?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes. Those are the firing tables that I used to calculate the dispersion pattern.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, we may make reference to this, these tables, again, but at this point could I ask they be admitted into evidence and given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the tables be given an exhibit number. They are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit 776, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel, on page 64 of your report and on page 76 in B/C/S is it correct that you reproduce certain portions of this firing table? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes. The two tables that I show include data from the firing table. The upper one for the 155 howitzer and lower down for the Orkan, for distances of 1620, 2530, ranging up to 50 kilometres in the first column, and in the second column we have the Vp values or figures and deviations, and the third column shows the Vd figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What does Vp stand for?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Vp stands for probable deviation of hits of dispersion in line, whereas Vd is range, dispersion in range and the probable deviations. So Vp and Vd and the inclination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just so we're clear about the terminology that's used, when you talk about dispersion in line, is that essentially how far to the left or to the right of the intended target the impact may actually fall? Is that what Vp stands for?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Let us assume that the mean target hits the target in the centre, the mean projectile hits the target in the centre. Impact is possible in line left or right for 4 Vp, left and right from the centre of impact, the mean impact point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And for Vd, am I -- do I understand that correctly that that's how far too long or too short the impact might be? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Once again, bearing in mine the mean impact point and from the mean impact the point the following is possible: Plus 4 Vd and minus 4 Vd.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I just want to understand Vd in normal language. What do you mean by dispersion in distance? Am I right to say that means the rocket could go too short or too long, or does it mean something else? That's what I want to understand.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Once again, we have the mean impact point. From that mean impact point the next projectile or following projectiles can fall from that mean impact point further, 4 Vd further. They can overshoot by 4 Vd, or, and this is equal probability, they can undershoot up to 4 Vp.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. A bit further along in this same section of your report you provide a table which gives various percentages, various probabilities about the effective probability of impact within the dispersion ellipse. Could you just please explain to us what's depicted in that table? This is on page 65 in English for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: The dispersion of impact in the overall pattern impact is uneven. If we go closer to the centre of the pattern of dispersion, we have a greater probability of accuracy of the next impact. If we move towards the edges, the possibility of accuracy decreases all the way up to plus/minus 4 Vd or Vp. Beyond those boundaries, we say that there were no hits because the probability of hitting the target beyond the boundaries of the ellipse is insignificant, negligible. Therefore, we have the table with the percentages. The percentages show the probability of hitting the target in individual areas of the ellipse of dispersion. We discussed dispersion by distance, and the SRP in the B/C/S or the mean impact point --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you for a moment. I apologise for the interruption, but there's perhaps a confusion with regard to language and it may be translation. In the English it reads the probability of hitting the target around this ellipse. Does probability show the probability of an impact or of hitting the target, which I understand to mean the centre, the thing that you aimed at. Can you just explain that so I'm clear on it, please?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: The table shows the probability of dispersion of hits are impact. If we have several projectiles within the boundaries of plus/minus 4 Vd, we will have all the impacts, but their degree of probability varies as opposed to the target. Therefore, we have greater probability of hitting the target towards the centre of the ellipse than we would have towards the boundaries, the outer parts of the ellipse.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think I understand you except when you say "there is a greater probability of hitting the target." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: That the projectile will fall within the boundaries of plus or minus 1 Vd. The percentage there is 50, meaning half of all the impacts would be between the range of plus or minus 1 Vd. As to the 82 per cent probability or chance, that is within plus or minus 2 Vd range. And we can go as far as 4 Vd. Therefore, we would have all impacts within the range of plus or minus 4 Vd.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And is the distribution of probability the same for Vp as it is for Vd? The table shows Vd, but does the same apply in principle to Vp?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Vd and Vp values differ, but the probability of impact is the same. The probability is the same to have a both plus/plus in regard of Vp and Vd and minus/minus. We could also have an impact on the left or on the right. The actual figure of Vp and Vd differ. With multiple rocket launchers, especially at the far end their range, Vp is always greater than Vd.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question not with regard to the particular values of Vp and Vd but with difference to this particular table that you've provided where you've explained there's a 50 per cent probability that the impact would be within plus or minus 1 Vd, is there also a 50 per cent probability that the impact would be within plus or minus 1 Vp? Is that the same in principle or is it different?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Both the dispersion by distance and by line obey the rules of the same law, meaning that the probability is equal in both distance and line.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just one more specific question then before I ask you to do this in a concrete contest, but just a more general question. The three columns of the firing tables which you've reproduced, one can see that both the Vp and Vd increase as you got to the bottom of the table. In ordinary language, please explain what that means.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: If we look at the table, we can conclude that as the distance grows, we also have greater dispersion in both Vp and Vd. We can see that at a 20 kilometre distance. Vp is 71 metres, which as Vd is 51. If we go up to 40 kilometres, Vp is 173, and Vd is 159. To me, it means that if we increase the range or the distance, we also increase the dispersion pattern.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me turn now to a concrete example or illustration of the principles which you've been explaining. If you look at page 78 in your version in B/C/S, and it starts at the bottom of page 65 in English and passes immediately to page 66, Lieutenant Colonel Poje, you give the example of an Orkan M87 fired from a distance of 40 kilometres from its target, and you provide a table here showing the probability of impacts. What I'd ask you to do is to walk us through that sort of step-by-step and explain us what is shown here in the table. I'd also mention to you that if you feel the need to draw or to show things, I do have scrap paper here, blank paper, so just ask me if you feel like you need that to give your explanations.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: I used the example of dispersion at the distance of 40.000 metres. Before me -- I have it before me, and perhaps it would be easier for me to clarify using that than using the table from the actual report. The principle is the same, but example I have is a textbook one explaining things in more detail and with greater clarity.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Please proceed then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Shouldn't the witness be using the ELMO then?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Perhaps I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Poje, just while we're setting up the ELMO, are you going to show us a part of your report or is this something -- something else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He's going to show us an example of shooting at 40 kilometres' distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But not -- not the calculations that exist in your report. Is that all right, Lieutenant Colonel, but something separate?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: No. That's the same calculation such as the one used in the report, but this is just put in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: In the report I cited an example of how to determine the dispersion pattern for the distance of 40 kilometres. From the firing tables referring to the distance of 40 kilometres, I took down the figures for Vp and Vd, and Vp is 73 -- 173, excuse me, and Vd is 159 metres. I will use this to explain the dispersion by distance only. I will only use the Vd figure. If we assume that the mean impact point is at the centre of the coordinate system and that the pattern of dispersion by distance, as we've said, in theory is plus/minus 4 Vd, this is plus 1, 2, 3 and 4, and minus 1, 2, 3 and 4 of Vd. We've already said that the Vd values for the distance of 40.000 metres is -- the figure is 159 metres. That means the distance between the mean impact point up to 1 Vd plus is 159 metres. And if we go the other way, the distance between the mean impact point and minus 1 Vd is also 159 metres. The probability of an impact within these two boundaries of plus and minus 1 Vd is 50 per cent. 25 per cent in the plus and 25 per cent in the minus. The entire dispersion pattern by distance equals plus/minus 4 Vd, which means that 4 Vd would be 4 times 159 metres, the total being of that of 636 metres. The same goes for the minus part of the table. Minus 4 Vd is also 636 metres. Within that range or within those limits of plus 632 and minus 632, we can have an impact looking from the mean impact point. That means that the axis of the distance dispersion equals 1.272 metres, that is plus/minus 4 Vd. In total that is 8 Vd. The outer limits of the ellipse for the dispersion are at 1.272 metres. The same goes for dispersion by line or bearing, to the left or to the right of plus/minus 4 Vp. Vp, the value is 173 metres by the firing -- according to the firing tables. That means the half or semi-axis of dispersion by line from the centre to its outer -- right outer edge is 692 metres. If we go to the left, because the probabilities are the same, is also 4 Vp or 692 metres. Which means that the axis of the dispersion pattern by line or bearing is plus/minus 4 Vp, rather, 8 Vp which equals 1.384 metres. That means that the semi-axis of the dispersion pattern amount to 692 times 632 metres. We have to take into account the axis of dispersion pattern, those being 1.384 times 1.272 metres. We can use an ellipse to show that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you for a moment? I'm sorry. I apologise for the interruption, but just before we move away from that document, a couple times a figure was at least translated as 632 metres, whereas what appears on the document is 636 metres. Could you please just clarify which it is, please. And it's on the previous document that you just discussed with us. If that could be placed back on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: It probably should have been 636 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Please continue with your explanation.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, 636 metres. That's the semi-axis of the dispersion pattern. We can also show the same dispersion pattern here as regards the distance of 40 kilometres, the axis of the dispersion pattern by distance and by line or bearing. The area of the ellipse is a bit less than 1.4 square kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that these documents each receive an exhibit number and be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The two documents will be received in evidence and could they be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit 777.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, will they be given one exhibit number or two exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: One.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: One number.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Lieutenant Colonel. We will return to that kind of calculation in just a moment, but in the meantime we can leave the ELMO there because we can use it again in just a moment. If we look at the very next section of your expert report, which is section 6.2.2, you discuss impact dispersion in the specific context on the attack on Zagreb on the 2nd and 3rd of May 1995. If you look at page 80 of your report which is page 67 in English, you make reference to a document there which is trial exhibit number 94 in this case and on the basis of that document you conclude: "That the firing position of the M87 Orkan SRL was in the sector, north of the village Slavsko Polje." And my question is if I were to show you a map of the area do you think you would be able to find Slavsko Polje on the map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where did you read, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It's the very first very sentence of 6.2.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I've seen it. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Lieutenant, Colonel do you think you'd be able to find Slavsko Polje on a map if I were to show you a map?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'd like to show the ERN 06002902. It's also in e-court but I think because I'm going to ask the witness to make a measurement it's easier if we work from hard copy. I would also note that this is page 20 of the atlas which is Exhibit 23 but it's been blown up for ease of use on the ELMO. If I could hand this to the witness, please. Actually, if you could put it on the ELMO that would be best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Do you have a grid reference, although it's blown up?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. It's in the top part of grid 3B --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: -- near the somewhat larger village of Vrgin Most or town of Vrgin Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel, if you can find Slavko Polje and underline it, please. Just underline the village name first.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Now, could you please put an X with a number 1 just north in the approximate location where the Orkan M87 was fired on the 2nd and 3rd of May, 1995? Just approximately.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And can you put a number 1 next to that X, please.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE

utterances.text: Now, if you look to the north, you'll see the greater city of Zagreb there, and if you could please put a number 2 approximately on the city of Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.text: Now, I've brought along a ruler, want the assistance of the usher I'll pass it to you. And I'd ask you just to draw a straight line connecting those two Xs at point 1 and point 2.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Poje, you'll see at the bottom of this map or page there's a scale there, and in fact it's provided in two ways. If we could -- if we could just show the bottom of the map on the ELMO, please. Is it possible that we can rotate the view of the ELMO so that everyone who is looking at the screen can see it right way up? utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, then using the graphic representation of the scale and the ruler that I provided you with, I'd like you to make an approximate measurement of -- of the line that you drew between points 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think that the ruler had overshot point 2 making something like point 2 Vd beyond the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel, I don't know if you heard His Honour's point. Yes. If you could re-measure to make sure it's precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note that the zero mark is not the very end of the ruler. So that could be what you saw?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About 49 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could you please write that distance next to the line that you drew there on the map. Just next to the line between 1 and 2, points 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes. I seen you've made a couple of marks before the 49, and that's to show that that's an approximate measurement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes, an approximate value, measurement, an approximate measurement, because we don't know the exact point from which the firing took place or the exact point where the target was. We know where the projectiles fell, but we haven't got the central point of impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And in your report it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Black, before you go on, I have just remarked that there's a variance in the spelling between the map grid B3 and what is in the report at 6.2.2. The report says the village of Savsko Polje. I think the report is the one that is inaccurate. Could I just confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Poje, is the correct name of the village Slavsko Polje or Savsko Polje?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: The correct name is Slavsko with an L, Slavsko Polje. There is a mistake there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask that this map as marked by the witness be given a number and admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The page of the map as marked by the witness is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. It will be Exhibit 778, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Poje, in your report, in that same section 6.2.2, you estimated that the distance was somewhere between 47 and 51 kilometres. Is that roughly consistent with the measurement which you've just made here in court?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes, it is. If we -- well, when we know that we don't know the exact coordinates and firing position, nor do we know the exact coordinates of the target aimed at, all we know is on the basis of documents the approximate place where the Orkan was sighted. We have information about where the projectiles fell, and then we can see that the distance or range is approximately 49, 50 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What I'd like you to do now is perform the same calculation of impact dispersion that you did before but now using the value 49 kilometres. I'd like you to walk us through that process. And to begin, if we could show again 65 ter number 2275, which has now been admitted into evidence as Exhibit 776. If we could see that on the e-court, please, and specifically page 98 of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: This is only in B/C/S, is? It.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, I was just going to mention that, Your Honours. There is to English translation because it's essentially tables of figures, and therefore we did not translate it into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Poje, if you look at it page of firing tables that we have before us, what values should we use for Vp and Vd to calculate the dispersion range at an impact of 49 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: If we take the range of 49 kilometres, then in the first column we find this range, 49.000 metres, if we go to columns 11 and 12. And at 49.000 metres we read the figures in column 11, Vd, and see that Vd at a range of 49.000 metres or 49 kilometres will be 243 metres. If we look at column 12, we can read the values of Vp, and that is 258 metres. 258 metres. So those are the basic parameters on the basis of which we are able to calculate the semi-axis of the dispersion ellipse and the semi-axis of the dispersion ellipse per range is 4 times Vd, 4 times 243.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Witness -- for the usher --

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Which is --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm just going to interrupt you. I'd just like to pass you a couple of pieces of blank paper and on the ELMO if you can walk us through these calculation and show us what you're doing, please.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: We said that the range, firing range, was 49.000 metres, or 49 kilometres. From the firing table, we look at the values of Vd and Vp. Vd at that distance for that range was shown in column 11, and that was 243 metres. Then we go to column 12 to read the Vp figure, the Vp value, which was 258 metres. So those are the basic parameters allowing us to calculate the dispersion impact. We said, and I'll draw this once again, this is the X and Y axis of the dispersion image, the coordinates, with a mean impact point where these two lines intersect, where the coordinates intersect. Now, looking at range, the dispersion impact is plus 4 Vd, and on the opposite side minus 4 Vd, which means that the semi-axis of the impact -- dispersion impact will be 4 times Vd, equals 4 times 243 metres, or that is equal to 972 metres. So this is it. 272 metres is this portion here. And the same applies in the opposite direction. Minus 4 Vd, 972 metres that way. One way and the other way. That is the axis of the ellipse of the dispersion impact in range, plus/minus Vd. And the same applies for the line, dispersion in line, the Vp. One, two, three, four sections, and one, two, three, four the other way. 4 Vp and minus 4 Vp. The semi-axis of the impact dispersion in line is equal to 4 Vp, which is 4 times 258 metres, which is equal to 1.032 metres. So it is 1.032 metres. And in the other direction it is the same figure. 1.032 metres in both directions. That means that the axis of the dispersion patterns are the same. In range it is 2 times 972 metres, and in line it is 2 times 1.032 metres, which means that it is a very high dispersion pattern. This is 972 times 1.032 metres. And it is possible to calculate the surface of the ellipse. This is what the ellipse would look like, roughly like this, roughly this shape. A little deformed, because the ratio between range and line. But it is an ellipse where the line dispersion is greater than the range dispersion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. Just a couple of questions to put it into ordinary language. The ellipse that you've drawn, that represent -- does that represent the area in which the probable impacts will land? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes. It is the ellipse where the projectiles will fall, where the impact will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And when firing the M87 Orkan at a range of 49 kilometres, how much to the let other to the right might the impact fall, to the left or to the right of the centre point?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Let us assume that the rocket opened, that the cluster warhead opened on the edge of the ellipse. And if we remember, we said that the surface of dispersion, according to a cluster warhead, when the cluster warhead opens up we said that the bomblets fall on a surface area of two hectares. That means that we can expect the projectiles to fall outside the area of the ellipse, outside the dispersion ellipse, the dark area. It might overshoot this dark area. This is the area in which we might expect the bomblets to drop.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think I understand, but I'm not sure you answered my question. Maybe you've gotten just ahead of me. My question is a simple one and I apologise if it sounds obvious but I want to understand these numbers in more ordinary language.
