Based on the calculations that you've done for us here, when firing from a range of 49 kilometres, how much to the left or to the right of the centre point might the rockets impact?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: From the calculations, from the central point we can go left and right by 1.032 metres. And in range, plus/minus from the central point of impact 972 metres. That means we can hit this area to the right 1.032 metres, and to the left 1.032 metres. And then range from the central point of impact plus 972 metres or minus 972 metres. So within that surface area is where all the projectiles will fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the explanation you were giving when you drew a circle on the perimeter of the ellipse, does that -- does that deal with each particular bomblet of the 288 that are in each warhead? Is that correct? Could you please explain that again since I interrupted you?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Let us assume that the cluster warheads opened along the edge of the dispersion ellipse, which means the following: The surface area on which the bomblets drop is two hectares. That means that it is still possible that part of the bomblets fall outside this area. Bearing in mind this dispersion pattern, it's a small portion, 100 metres. So some of the bomblets can fall outside the circumference of that ellipse.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you for your explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, could this be given a number and admitted into evidence now, please, this sketch paper where he's done this calculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The sketch drawing is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 779, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Poje, in principle could this same exercise, these same calculations, be repeated for any, any distance, be it 47 kilometres, 49 and a half kilometres, any distance that you find for the distance from which the rockets were launched on the 2nd and 3rd of May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: If we know the distance or range, then in the firing tables we can read the values for Vd and Vp. And as we saw on the basis of the calculations we did a moment ago, it is possible to calculate this for any distance, any range at all. You can calculate the dispersion pattern for any range or distance you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I'm going to move away from the specific topic of impact dispersion. I'm going to ask you to look at section 5 of your expert report which addresses the use of artillery in populated areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, this appears on page 60 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Have you found that, Lieutenant Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And is that on page 71? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What kind of considerations determine whether or not and how you might use artillery in a populated -- against a populated area? What things must be taken into account?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: In that respect, I tried to present the use of the artillery in populated areas by using the rules of artillery firing which records how artillery should be used in populated areas. A large number of factors influence the use of artillery in a populated area, your choice. The size of a town will be an influencing factor. And a town or city is a target in which it is difficult to pinpoint various targets because there are high-rise buildings, low buildings. Visibility differs. Visibility is relatively pretty poor in a town or city. Then you have positions, firing positions. There is a poor communication possibilities. That is why when we think of an attack on a populated area indirect firing is usually used to detect targets, because that is more effective and more precise. Any form of direct fire is more precise, especially if it is done at great distances.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me stop you there and just ask you about -- a question about that last answer. Which -- which is more precise, indirect fire or direct fire?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: At all times direct fire is more precise than indirect fire, because with direct fire you can see the target and you can have a direct effect on the firing itself because you can see the target. When you have indirect fire, the target cannot be seen from the firing position, but you use an auxiliary point to target. And the results of firing are viewed from an observation point or are not observed at all. So there's an essential difference between direct fire and indirect fire. Direct fire from the position the weapon is located. You can see the target and you can fire at the target and hit it. When you have indirect fire you use your sights to target an auxiliary point, and then you use observation points to look at the effects of your firing. Or there can be no observation all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Which type of firing was at issue on the 2nd and 3rd of May, 1995? Was that direct firing or indirect firing by the M87 Orkan?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: On the 2nd and 3rd of May, 1995, indirect fire was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When you were explaining before about artillery attacks around populated areas, which is generally preferred, direct firing or indirect firing?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: If possible, when attacking a populated area direct firing is resorted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In the decision whether to use artillery against a populated area, does the choice of weapon or the type of weapon affect the decision-making? Is that a decision that should be taken into account?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: When you're choosing your weapons and the type of firing you're going to resort to, you must take care to select the weapons which under given conditions has the least dispersion and is the most precise. That means that when attacking a town, if possible you would use direct firing and weapons that are adapted to direct firing, because more precise weapons mean less -- mean less dispersion and less possibility of your impact being outside the target being targeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In section 5.2, it's the second paragraph there, page 61 in the English version, you say that multiple-barrel rocket launchers in general are "unsuitable for firing on targets in populated areas." Why is that so?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Because there is high dispersion when using multiple-barrel rocket launchers, not only Orkan but others two. And we saw with the two examples just how high that dispersion is at a distance or range is at 49 kilometres or 49.000 metres, which means there is great probability that many of the projectiles fall outside the designated target. And at least once a year at the military academy I demonstrated firing from a multiple-barrel rocket launcher for the cadets of the military academy as an exercise, and I was able to see it. Not only looking at it from the tables and the calculations, I showed them in practical terms that the dispersion is extremely high. And that is why, because of this high dispersion, you have a high probability of hitting targets outside your principal target, and that is why it is not suited to populated areas. And otherwise, when using a multiple-barrel rocket launcher, you must look at the safety zone so that you don't inflict injuries on your own forces precisely because of this high level dispersion. So the main reason why you would not use a multiple-barrel rocket launcher in populated areas is because of this high level of dispersion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Poje, based on all the information you've given us today and on your own military experience and your expertise in the field of artillery, do you have an opinion regarding the appropriateness of firing the Orkan M87 at Zagreb on the 2nd and 3rd of May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: I would put it this way: Even if there might have been military targets within Zagreb and if their -- and if the intention was to target them, I don't think that this should have been chosen, to act against those targets. And I said this a moment ago. When making the decision about using Orkan for the town of Zagreb, which is a populated area, relatively densely populated area, at a time when life was going on normally in Zagreb, one could have expected that even if you targeted a military target you should not do so when that military target was in the town and in this case the city of Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And just one question before we take another break. Perhaps this is obvious, but I want you to make it clear. What was the risk? Why was it inappropriate? What was the danger of firing the Orkan at the city centre of Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: As I've already said, if the aim was a military target, hitting a military target, because of the high dispersion that kind of targeting was not suited, because according -- I was able to calculate, and everybody else could have calculated the dispersion pattern and could have arrived at the conclusion that the area where the rockets would fall would be a large area with high possibilities of overshooting or undershooting the military targets and hitting civilian facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps that's an appropriate time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Black. We'll take a break, and we'll come back at half past twelve. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Poje, I'd like to ask you now to turn to section 6.1 of your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: This begins, Your Honours, in the English version just at the beginning -- at the bottom, excuse me, of page 61, and then really on page 62.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think it's around page 73 of the B/C/S version, Lieutenant Colonel. In this section of your report you refer to a number of documents, and I'd like to show a few of those documents to you now. The first one is 65 ter number 1887. If we could please see that on e-court. Lieutenant Colonel, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I made use of this document when compiling the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And in fact, you reproduced parts of this document in your report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes. The part of it pertaining to the multiple rocket launcher Orkan. That's what I used in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could look at -- it's page 13 in e-court of the B/C/S version, although the number at the top of the page will say page 12, and it's page 13 in the English version. If we could pull that up, please. Lieutenant Colonel Poje, if you look at page, in particular 5.8, subsection 2. If you would scroll down, please. Is this -- you don't need to read anything out loud, but is this part of the document what you relied on in your report?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes, it is. This is what I basically copied into my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And what does this tell us about the command and control of the M87 Orkan?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: This states that the Orkan stating here AG VBR was part of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And just so it's clear, which armed forces? The General Staff of which armed forces?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: The General Staff of the Serb armed forces of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document receive a number and be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 780, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The next document is 65 ter number 1888. And if that could please be brought up on the screen and in fact if we could move to page 11 in e-court in the English. It's page 6 in B/C/S in e-court, although again I note it has the number 4 at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, by way of explanation, some of these 65 ter exhibits appear to have some tables and things we've matched together. That's why the page numbers don't always correspond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Page in English we must go to page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Page 11, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Poje, do you recognise this document, and if --

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Is this the document -- the next document that's referred to in your report? Is that correct? And if we could scroll down the page in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Keep going. Continue to section 4 and then subsection 2. That's perfect. Thank you very much. Again, Lieutenant Colonel, you don't need to read out any passages from this, but if you would please explain what the document demonstrates about the command and control of the Orkan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, when you say section 4, subsection 2, what are you referring to on that page 11?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me check my English version, Your Honour, so I can make sure I'm pointing you to the correct page. Yes. I believe it's at the very top of the page. Right, the section 4 doesn't show on page 11, it's the first part at the top of page 11 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel, what does this document show us about the command and control of the Orkan?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: This item states that the Orkan unit is part of the 7th mixed artillery regiment and its use can only be approved by the commander of the Main Staff of the SVK.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could this document also be given a number and admitted, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 781, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The next I believe final document that we'll look at is trial Exhibit 92. If that could be -- please be put on the screen, and it will be the first page both in B/C/S and in English that we're interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Poje, do you recognise the document that's on the screen now in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can you read -- before we go down, is it -- can you read the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: The 1st of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you look at paragraph 1. So if we can scroll down a little bit, what does this document tell us about the command and control of the M87 Orkan?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: In item 1 of the order: "It is stated that the Orkan squad, together with the military police squad, as well as the S-1 squad from the 7th Corps will be ready to act as I order." It literally states "according to my order."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down the page, who issued this order?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: The order was signed by Commander Lieutenant General Celeketic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And do you know what position General Celeketic had at this time in May 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: I think he was Chief of Staff of the Main Staff of the SVK.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, that's all we need with that document. It's already in evidence, Your Honour, so we don't need to move it in again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Poje, on the basis of these documents that we've just looked at as well as your own military experience and your expertise in the field of artillery, what conclusion did you reach about who commanded and controlled the SVK M87 Orkans when they fired upon Zagreb on the 2nd and 3rd of May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: In all the documents we've just mentioned, it is stated that the Orkan squad can only be used on orders of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do they -- do they refer to anyone in particular in the Main Staff or just the Main Staff generally?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: It is mentioned. And the use of the Orkan squad as well as the tasks for the squad are to be issued by the commander of the Main Staff or Colonel Djilas.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know what position Colonel Djilas had? If you don't know that's fine, but just if you do know.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Poje, you served in the military for more than 30 years. You've specialised in artillery issues, and I believe at one point you testified you commanded some artillery formation. In your opinion, would the people who ordered the use of the M87 Orkan on the 2nd and 3rd of May, 1995, would they have been aware of the risk to civilians which you discussed earlier?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: We need to propose that perhaps not everyone is familiar with the consequences of the use of the Orkan, and some of those people may have been the people who decided to use it. And the people who made the decision on the use may not have been familiar with its consequences, but in any case, they should have informed themselves. Within the Main Staff there must be a department or another body in possession of the necessary expert knowledge as to advise them what would happen if they used the Orkan against, say, Zagreb. One needn't know everything, but then you have to inquire. You have to ask someone who does before you make the final decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And as a matter of ordinary military practice, do commanders in fact inform themselves before they take this kind of decision?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: In principle, yes. The commander is supposed to use certain units, inter alia, the use of artillery units. Also, the commander must be familiarised with the use of such weapons, save for such a situation in which there is absolutely no time or under the circumstances which you cannot possibly get that information from anyone. But I don't think that applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That completes my direct examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Black. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Poje. My name is Mr. Milovancevic, Defence counsel for the Accused Mr. Milan Martic, and we are about to commence with your cross-examination. You have found in similar situations -- you have found yourself in similar situations before, but I still need to ask you to pause between question and answer. This goes for both myself and you so that the interpreters could do their work. Thank you. From your particulars, I could see that you completed the military academy in 1971, the academy of the land forces in Belgrade. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I can also see there between the -- 1971 and 1975 you commanded a mortar battery. What was your rank at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: I was 2nd lieutenant or lieutenant. I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Between 1975 and 1978, according to your report, it states that you commanded an anti-armour battery of 105-millimetre calibre. What was your rank then?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: I believe by the time I left that duty I was holding the rank of captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As regards this anti-armour gun battery, what is it exactly?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: It is a unit in which there are six anti-armour guns or cannons of 120-millimetre T12 guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Between 1978 and 1980 -- 91, you state that you lectured at the army school centre in Zadar. I believe it was a part of the JNA educational system?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: There you taught the theory of firing and artillery firing rules for a year at the school for reserve officers and two years to the cadets of the military academy as well as two years for the commanders of artillery battalion. What was your rank at the end of that period?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: I had taught for ten years at the academy and two years at the course for the commanders of artillery battalions, and when I left I held the rank of lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I can also see here that in 1984, you graduated from the Command Staff Academy as an external 4th class student. It is an eminent military school, and it is higher than the military academy that you had graduated at previously.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you left the JNA in 1991, when you did that upon your own request, you found employment with the military school centre, and you taught military topography, artillery firing, topographic and geodesic support for artillery units. And now you are the head of the centre for educational work.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And you are still a lieutenant colonel. For how long?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you should ask that to someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Am I correct in saying that you've been a lieutenant colonel ever since 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your long career as an artilleryman, you stated that at live fire exercises and other exercises you fired around 15.000 projectiles. According to the calibres I can see the greatest calibre you worked with was one of 155 millimetres, which means you have not used the Orkan?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do I interpret your answer correctly, that being that as regards its practical use and the practical impact, you have no direct experience?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: At my school centre we haven't used the Orkan a single time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. According to your military education and the degree you hold, you -- you specialised in artillery, and you were a high-ranking officer. I wanted to ask you something about the artillery itself, the types of artillery, types of usage. Therefore, we are now to go into the topic that hasn't been touched upon by the Prosecutor. In chapter 3 you talk about the technical aspects of artillery. You talk about fire support, artillery fire support, and you state there that it is the fire action of artillery against enemy forces for the purpose of supporting one's own forces in combat. You also state that such support includes direct and general fire support?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, could you please give us an indication of the page you're at so we can be following when you cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That is at the beginning of the report. In the B/C/S, that is page 7, right after "Background information". In the English that's page 6, after chapter 3. We see chapter 3 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: After chapter 2 there is chapter 3, technical aspects of artillery fire supports. That's where I was reading from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If artillery as a branch of the armed forces can support its own forces in combat, be it directly or generally -- perhaps we should clarify one thing first. The use of the Orkan, in your terms does this represent the support to one's own forces, to the forces of the SVK?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Probably so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the answer was yes. Thank you. When explaining the impact of the use of artillery and when you say that it can include direct artillery fire support, you state that that fire support is the fire action of establishment of artillery, as opposed to general fire support. General fire support provides support which has a general effect on the activity of the supported unit. This usage of the Orkan, could that fall under the general artillery fire support?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, am I correct in saying that such support had a general effect on the activity of the armed forces of the SVK?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we're talking about the type of fire support and the use of artillery, we also mentioned the use of the rocket system the Orkan, and in item 3.1, in the last sentence you say that certain rockets group comprise or can be included in the support. There you specify battalions, artillery battalions, and the use of multiple rocket launchers. Does that mean that the Orkan as a multiple rocket launcher is part of such general artillery fire support units?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As regards the topic we've covered so far, it seems logical for me to ask, and you've touched upon it in your report, about the classification of artillery, and there you state that it is a branch of the army with great firepower. On the next page, in chapter 3.2, you state that according to the ballistic characteristics artillery can be divided into classical artillery and rocket artillery, or conventional artillery and rocket artillery. That is on the next page. As regards this distinction, is it correct that guns, howitzers, and gun-howitzers as well as mortars comprise this conventional artillery, whereas multiple rocket launcher fall within the category of the so-called rocket artillery? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes. I've stated that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you move on to the calibre of artillery, meaning you also provided the breakdown according to the calibre, you state that the conventional artillery can be divided as small, medium, and large calibre artillery. According to its range, artillery is divided into conventional artillery and rocket artillery. Regarding that, I'm interested in one piece of information pertaining to the range of the rocket artillery. Multiple rocket launchers fall under the rocket artillery category, and there you stayed they are divided into three groups, those of small, medium, and long range. Which group does the Orkan belong to?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Realistically speaking, it would be within the category of fire support of small range or short range, although it can reach up to 50 kilometres. It is somewhere in between short and medium-range artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: To put this in a context, when you talk about the range of rocket artillery you state that short-range artillery includes all multiple rocket launchers of range up to 10, then medium up to 20 -- up to 200, and long range above 200.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers please not overlap and pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Slower. And I think the numbers are differing from the numbers in the expert report where it says short-range up to 50 kilometres, mid-range between 50 and 200, and long-range over 200 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poje, it seems I have explained you, but I am the one violating the speed. Thank you, Your Honour, for your reminder. So as to clear -- clear up the transcript, short-range multiple rocket launchers can reached up to 50 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Multiple rocket launchers of medium range can reach between 50 and 200 kilometres; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And the third group is that of long range, over 200 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes. If I may, this does not only include multiple rocket launchers but rockets in general, including ground-to-ground rockets as well as other types of rockets including multiple rocket launchers and their ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in that same chapter, 3.2, where you speak about the classification of artillery, underneath what we've just said about range and rocket support there's something that is referred to as conventional artillery, and you distinguish between guns, howitzers, and gun-howitzers. That is conventional artillery and you differentiate that between that and the rocket artillery. And when you refer to rocket artillery, you mean the multiple-barrel rocket launcher called Orkan. That belongs to rocket artillery, does it?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes I looked at anti-armour missile launchers and the multiple-barrel rocket types, and the ground to ground systems I did not deal with specifically here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in the last paragraph before we come to the next point 3.3 definitions and types of artillery firing, when you say multiple rocket launchers are weapons with -- launched from barrels, you differentiate between two types of multiple rocket launchers, do you not?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what the literature describes as well. The rocket launchers and the rail launched multiple rocket launchers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, the tube-launched multiple rocket launchers, how many barrels or tubes?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Twelve.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel, perhaps it would be interesting to look at the following question: What is the -- why were multi-barrelled rocket launchers devised as opposed to conventional artillery? How many rocket launchers can replace classical or conventional guns, for example?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: If we take a look at Orkan, the Orkan system, with 12 tubes, that means that it replaces -- we're talking about one launcher, one 12-tube or 12-barrelled launcher, a system like that can replace 12 conventional weapons because it's 12 tubes, 12-barrelled, which means two batteries, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that it's -- that it has the same effect as 12 guns of the same calibre?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Could the witness answer why the multi-barrelled rocket launcher was designed? That was a question Defence counsel has asked, but I don't believe it has been appropriately responded to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel, you've heard the question from Judge Nosworthy. The question was why the multiple-barrel rocket launcher was designed in the first place. Could we have a specific answer, and tell us when it first came into existence, whether it is a new weapon, whether the Orkan was the first weapon of that type, and why it was designed and mid in the first place?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: The multiple-barrelled rocket launchers were used for fire support in the first place because they were highly effective and efficient. The Yugoslav People's Army, before Orkan, had two types of multi- barrelled rocket launchers. They were called Plamen and Oganj. They were 128-millimetres and they had 30 barrels or tubes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: To have a complete answer to the question I asked you, I'll put it this way: Am I right in saying that a multiple-barrel rocket launcher as an artillery piece has the advantage over conventional weapons because one piece enables effective, sudden, and strong fire, firepower, which is the equivalent of one or more batteries of guns? So in that sense it has the advantage, because there's only one vehicle, one truck that you need. And otherwise, you would need several artillery units to obtain the same effect. So is that why this multi-barrelled rocket launcher was designed?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Precisely so, because you have one system which can replace a number of conventional pieces and weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in view of the type of charge, the warheads, the explosives it uses, does the multiple-barrel rocket launcher come under normal artillery pieces? It's not nuclear, is it? It's normally the classical type.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Well, it is conventional, classical artillery, if you compare it to nuclear weapons. So it's not a nuclear weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I meant. It's conventional, a conventional weapon?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Now let us look at section 3.3, chapter 3.3, definitions and types of artillery firings. And as this weapon comes under artillery weapons, you speak of two types of firings, direct fire at a target visible and indirect fire at a target not visible. So I'm interested, there's a third type of fire but I'm interested in the first two, direct an indirect. Can you tell us what we mean by direct fire?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: I think I've already answered that question. Direct fire is fire that is directed at a target visible from the location of the target piece. The aiming is direct and the results of the firing are observed from the firing position, the weapon location. When you have indirect fire, the target which is not visible from the location of the artillery piece and is not observed --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we've had a description of direct fire from you. Now, as a method of firing, does it refer specifically to a gun? It is guns that are used for direct fire as an artillery piece?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes, guns and howitzers as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, taking all this into account, in addition to direct fire using conventional artillery pieces, guns, howitzers, mortars, can we target indirectly as well? So can conventional weapons be used to fire indirectly as well?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, indirect fire is used when the target is not visible, you said, but when it has to be aimed at indirectly by means of an auxiliary aim point and the results of the firing are observed from an observation post or are not observed, and you said you can use a gun as well for indirect firing. Now, do you still stand by what you said that the multiple-barrelled rocket launchers are artillery pieces which are exclusively used for indirect fire?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes, indirect fire always.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So is it true that multi-barrel rocket launchers do not fire directly but because of their properties they target indirectly 59 long range, long distances?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes, all multiple-barrelled rocket launchers, not only the Orkan type. We have other ones whose range is under eight kilometres, but it is all through indirect fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Lieutenant Colonel. And then in that same paragraph, same chapter, you differentiate on page 12, that's 12 of the B/C/S, when we come to the type of fire, you speak of the types of projectiles, artillery projectiles, and the fuse-setting method, and you speak of impact fire, ricochet fire, and delayed fire. Can you tell us what kind of firing is applied with the Orkan?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: The Orkan uses timed or delayed fire, because the explosion of the warhead takes place before the projectile in its trajectory hits the target or the point of impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That brings us to a very interesting point now, Lieutenant Colonel, and we mustn't get this mixed up. There mustn't be a misunderstanding. Specifically, the multiple-barrel Orkan rocket launcher we're talking about now, the Orkan, it was designed in such a way as it can impact with its whole mass?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Not in principle, because the explosion and the release of the bomblets occurs during the trajectory before the missile impacts, before it hits the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: May we have Exhibit 771 placed on the e-court, please. And before the document appears, I'd just like to tell you that it's the schematic, the diagram of the dispersion of the Orkan projectiles 800 to 1.000 metres above ground. I'm sure you will remember that diagram. On the diagram we can see a trajectory of a projectile, which at a certain height opens and let's out the bomblets. You spoke about the delayed fire on the fuse. You meant a delayed fire at an altitude of 800 to 1.000 metres on that trajectory when that happens?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, to go back to the diagram. At the point where the warhead opens up, one of the bomblets explodes?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: No. Once the warhead opens up the bomblets dispersion and start falling towards the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So will you remind us, please, how many bomblets does this Orkan weapon have?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: 288 bomblets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on this diagram, the diagram we have on the monitor, we see the rocket as it is firing, and the mechanism opens up the warhead and these bomblets are released. And we have established that at the point of dispersion the bomblets do not explode. Now, my question in that regard is when do the bomblets actually explode?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: When the bomblets are falling, we say that they are stabilised with the textile band. At the same time, those bands set off the fuse, the bomblets fuse, and the bomblets explode at the point of contact, at the point the bomblet makes contact with the obstacle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in connection with that answer, my next question is the following: The point we see captured on the diagram, is it the technical point in the construction of this rocket which enables the bomblets, which are supposed to act and have their effect, to disperse over a larger area? Is that what it means?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes. The -- we timed the fuse, delayed the fire, and it -- depending on the range of firing at a target the cluster warhead opens up and the bomblets drop down onto the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just follow the argument as you go along. By bomblets, what do we refer to? Do we refer to those little small balls that we saw around that exhibit, or do we mean the exhibit itself? It's the whole exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you for asking that. It's quite a very logical question, and that is the point I've arrived at. So with your permission I'd like to ask my next questions, and I think the witness will provide an answer to what you've just asked. Could the witness please be shown Exhibit 774 again, please, and it is the bomblet itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel, the reason I've asked them to bring that bomblet to you is the following: What you see on our monitor, the opening of the warhead and the dispersion, is that the point at which by delayed fire these kind -- this kind of droplet false on the target?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: When the warhead, cluster warhead opens, out of the warhead you have 288 such bomblets, 288 of this kind of bomblet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Lieutenant Colonel. So we're at an altitude of 800 to 1.000 metres and you have these 288 bomblets of this kind with the bands that fall in principle vertically downwards towards the ground that's how they're constructed is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it also right that none of these droplets explode until it hits the target only when it hits the target it explodes?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: In principle the bomblets explode on impact with the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I will have to slow down, Your Honour. I do apologise. Please stop me, because of course the witness and I speak the same language we understand each other, so we seem to run ahead of ourselves. But as we're discussing bomblets --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You just asked me to stop you. May I stop you, please. Now, that bomblet explodes on impact. Is it at the time of that explosion that the little marbles that injure people come out, or when do they come out? Those little ones that are wrapped around the bomblet with the plastic -- transparent plastic, cellophane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness seems to be waiting for me to ask him a question, but you are asking the question directly of the witness. That's what I understood. I don't have to intervene. You are asking the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. If you can --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already said once today. When the cluster warhead opens up, 288 bomblets start falling towards the target. It is -- they are stabilised by this textile band. It stabilises the bomblet so that it doesn't fly over a larger area. And this sets off a fuse activating the bomblet once the bomblet impacts, hits the target, hits an obstacle. When it impacts, hits the obstacle, because of the explosive inside it, part of the explosive is spent to disperse the little balls or pellets in a circle all around, and this affects live force or humans. It is not very effective. These little balls or pellets aren't very effective. They're not too lethal. The gases created by the explosion are focused into a point and pierce the obstacle, pierce the target. I hope that makes it clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poje, since the activation of the bomblet as being part of the rocket initiated a series of questions, it seems important that we clarify it all the way. Did we, therefore, manage to establish that at the moment whether at the elevation of 800 to 1.000 metres the casing of the rocket opens up, the bomblets are freed and dispersed falling downwards to the ground; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As regards the bomblet, you stated it had a fragmentation, a shaped fragmentation charge.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And cumulative as well. You also stated that the band is used as a stabiliser as well as arms the fuse. Is it correct that the bomblet explodes upon impact when it hits the target, an obstacle?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes. It explodes at the moment it touches an obstacle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you remind us yet again how many bomblets there are in a rocket?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: A warhead there are 288 such bomblets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You stated that the band arms the fuse. Does that mean that the 288 bomblets has such a band stabilising it and arm the fuse?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: All bomblets have such a band stabiliser.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that such a bomblet, and you will tell us how heavy it is, is it possible for it to go off without a fuse?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: No, not without a fuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What creates the explosion once it impacts a surface?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: The bomblet has a fuse. The fuse activates the initial charge which in turn activates the explosive charge in the bomblet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, each bomblet has a fuse, and as regards the activation of the bomblet, is the fuse an actual mechanism with a small explosive charge, and when that goes off the entire charge is activated?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes. In the fuse there is the so-called initial powder charge, which is very sensitive to movement or to impact. It goes off, and based on that small explosion the larger explosion of the charge in the bomblet occurs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, after the warhead has opened up at the elevation of about 1.000 metres, the bomblets drop towards the target. They hit a surface, the fuse goes off, and then each of the bomblets is activated.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If we've clarified this in sufficient detail, we may move on to some other characteristic of the bomblet. When you mentioned the types of charge for artillery projectiles, you mentioned artillery projectiles which can be -- which can have fragmentation characteristics, impact characteristics, and for this one you stated that it had -- was of cumulative and fragmentation nature.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the rockets used to attack Zagreb had such bomblets with both fragmentation and cumulative characteristics?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: From all the references including the firing tables, the warhead, the cluster warhead, is described mentioning two types of cluster warheads. One is with fragmentation cumulative charge, being this one, and other one with anti-armour explosive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We now described the type of warheads, but now let us go -- let us go back to the topic itself. The bomblet that you have in your hand is one of those which was dispersed at 800 to 1.000 metres. It falls down, initiates contact with the surface and sets off the fuse initiating activating the initial charge. You stated that the bomblet initiates a funnel effect with a focus which can pierce armour?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. The explosive charge partly disperses the pellets, partly concentrates the fumes created by the explosion to create this funnel cumulative effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Am I right to say that each of the bomblets has an internal powder charge -- not powder but explosive charge, and you said that in principle that explosive is trotyl?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Upon the activation of the fuse, the explosive explodes creating a high field of pressure focusing on only one point, achieving a cumulative effect. Is that also one of the things that happens during the explosion?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: One way of the bomblet to explode is to have such a cumulative characteristic, because it was designed in that way. All the gases created and all the pressure created is focused in one point. It is not the ideal point, but we try to achieve the focus by the design of the bomblet itself and the material that is used in order to have the focus on the surface or on the target itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask interpreters to warn me yet again if I hurry since we speak the same language. I'm talking about the cumulative charge and the effect that occurs when the bomb goes on. There is another feature you've mentioned. Am I right to say that a part of the explosive charge in each bomblet, in addition to the cumulative effect, also has a fragmentation effect? The sheeting is destroyed, and the pellets are dispersed in the diameter of some 10 metres, injuring personnel?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes. A part of it has the cumulative effect focusing on the surface, whereas the other portion of the explosion has the fragmentation effect dispersing the 420 pellets covering the area of some 10 metres. References mention 10 metres or more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Since we are discussing the technical characteristics of the Orkan, up until now we discussed the rocket with the warhead, which has the cumulative and fragmentation effect containing the bomblets such as this one; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The other type of the Orkan rocket has a different charge. To be more specific, is it correct that the Orkan rocket can have only two types of war let's, the one with cumulative effects, such as this one, and a warhead used for anti- -- to pierce armour? These are anti-tank shells?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes. One type of warhead has a shaped charge and fragmentation and bomblets and the other one is used to pierce armour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: To clarify other thing: During your testimony in chief a question was asked of you from which we could conclude that such a charge would, in turn, mean that there is a cluster warhead. Am I right to say that the multiple rocket launcher Orkan has two types of warheads and both of them are warheads?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: I think I mentioned that, on several occasions, that the Orkan uses the rocket which has two types of cluster warheads. One is the type we've discussed with the fragmentation and cumulative bomblets, and the other one which has 24 anti-tank shells. As far as I know, the Orkan uses exclusively only cluster ammunition. Although, there was some mention of designing a different type of warhead, but it never came about, especially in the references I used for this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So as to discuss this further in detail because this is a very technical matter with which attorneys seldom have use of, but this warhead with the cumulative fragmentation charge -- I apologise I'll start again. Had the anti-tank shells have been used would the effect have been the same with the fragmentation cumulative warhead? Would it also disperse pellets at the height of 800 to 1.000 metres?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: The point is that they are equipped differently. In one type of warhead there are fragmentation cumulative bomblets aimed at personnel and tanks, armoured personnel carriers, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The other type of warhead contains 24 anti-tank shells. This other type of warhead is used for barrage fire or preventive fire against armour units when enemy tanks advance, to create a sort of a minefield in front of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As regards that answer of yours, does that mean that the use of such a type of warhead against Zagreb would presuppose the dispersion of anti-tank shells on that area?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes. Instead of the bomblets we would have had the anti-tank shellings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are both charges cluster charges?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Concerning the tactical and technical characteristics of the bomblets, you said it appears reinforced steel up to 60 millimetres. Just to have an illustration of that, it is that thick, 6 centimetres of steel. You say that this little contraption, I don't know why it's called a bomblet, why we refer to it by a diminutive, but it is used against all known standard types of tank?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes. The references specify that, and perhaps we should give it some credit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is there any difference between reinforced steel and plain steel?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What would be the ratio in terms of thickness? Say, six centimetres of reinforced steel, how much would that be in plain steel?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Am I correct if I say that it would be 10 to 12 centimetres of ordinary steel?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: I don't know. Some comparisons were made, but I can only speculate now. I may have overheard such piece of information, but I don't know now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I won't insist any further then. I have another question for you. Since -- since the effect of the bomblet happens on impact, piercing 6 centimetres of reinforced steel, what would be the equivalent if we discuss, for example, the soil or a tree or a wall? How thick would a wall have to be to correspond to six centimetres of reinforced steel?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: I can't say specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: One can find the reference to 15 to 20 centimetres of a brick wall and up to 30 centimetres of wood and more for the earth. Do you remember any such comparisons comparing the ability of the projectile and its differences if applied against steel or some other material?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: I can't recall the specific numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If such a bomblet can pierce the turret of the latest tank, can it also inflict heavy damage on a building, say of the Ministry of Defence, or can it be used against other materiel and equipment?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This type of rocket, has it been designed to use exactly for that? That's why it's called cumulative fragmentation rocket. That was its basic intention?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Its basic purpose was to be used against personnel and equipment including tanks, personnel carriers, buildings if need be, and some other facilities that can be used for military purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As regards these other facilities, we are going to come to that as well in our cross-examination. In chapter 3.4, you mentioned definition and types of targets. That is page 13 of the B/C/S, and the next chapter in the English after "Types of firing." You state there that "an artillery target is any element of the enemy's combat formation (feature or structure) which it is appropriate and cost effective to attack with artillery." Therefore, my question is as follows: This sentence, can this also be applied to the use of the Arkan, any feature or structure which is appropriate and cost-effective to attack with artillery?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it stated in the artillery firing rules. It is an artillery target, be it a gun or the Orkan or the earth-to-earth rocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You've spent a number of years with the artillery, and you quote here in footnote number 4, Artillery Firing Rules. And you mention the Artillery Firing Rules of the artillery directorate of the General Staff of the armed force of the SFRY, that is of the JNA of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes. And I was also one of the authors of the Artillery Firing Rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So this provision of the Artillery Firing Rules according to which the artillery target is any element of the enemy's combat formation which it is appropriate and cost effective to attack, it is not your own conclusion. It is one of the basic principles of the deployment of the artillery as a branch of the Armed Services; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In continuation, you say what the target is in the sense of artillery firing rules. You go on to explain that it is a rectangular land or water area enclosing the physical target. You go on to speak about the coordinates. Now, in that connection I would like to ask you the following question: Are all targets of the same importance or is there a division into tactical targets, operational targets, and strategical targets?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Targets are divided into tactical, operational, or strategic, according to tactical, operational, or strategic importance.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, within the operational importance or strategic importance, can that be the headquarters of the Supreme Command, for example, the General Staff, the Ministry of Defence from which the operations are directed against forces.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: In principle, yes, they can be any of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Furthermore, in your expert findings you say that targets are target based on weapon range. Now, with respect to that, and we're looking at page 14 of the B/C/S, it is 3.4, targets can be fired at if it is within the range of the artillery piece. That's quite logical, of course. You can't target a targets that is beyond a weapon's range. Now, in the case of Orkan, was that within the range of the artillery piece?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you refer to targets, you divide them up according to structure and divide them up as individual or elementary, single or elementary targets, heavy weapon, tank, launcher, bunker, et cetera, or as group targets. And my question for you is this: The characteristics, tactical, technical characteristics of the Orkan system, are they such that it is appropriate for targeting group targets?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: In view of the dispersion diagram, the Orkan was designed for large-scale group targets, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 17 of the B/C/S, or, rather, the next chapter in your report point 3.5 entitled artillery ammunition, that's what I'd like to refer you to now, and you speak about artillery ammunition and expound upon a topic that we already discussed before discussing this particular chapter when we spoke about the ammunition for the Orkan rocket launcher system. In this chapter, for artillery ammunition you say that there is a projectile that must be launched at a certain distance in order to realise the assignment. Is that the principle that is applied to the Orkan rocket system as well?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes, it is. The only difference being that in the rocket systems there is a rocket motor which ensures this, whereas with the conventional weaponry it is -- the projectile is ejected from a barrel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think this would be an opportune moment to break for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is indeed. We reconvene tomorrow morning at 9.00. Court adjourn --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry to rise and to interrupt. If I could have three minutes of the Court's time. I just want to raise a small matter that pertains to tomorrow's sitting and I would just like a moment. The next witness we were supposed to have after this witness was supposed to be Slobodan Lazarevic. We have decided to drop him as a witness and move on to the next witness, MM-80, and then continue with the list. This is not based on anything new that we've learned about the witness. It's really based on three factors. The first is that this witness has always been more or less a background witness and has added only a very narrow piece. In fact, his evidence was admitted via 92 bis and he was really here just for very limited direct and mostly for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who is that, Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Lazarevic. So that's the first reason. And the second reason is, of course, we're always looking for opportunities to streamline our case and move the case along. The third reason, Your Honour, is that in meeting with the witness the very narrow piece we were interested in, I've spoken to him about it, I find his memory not to be very good on that point, a bit vague. Not that it's any different than what it was, it's just more vague. So for those reasons, the Prosecution has decided drop him as a witness. Now, what this means is his evidence and the exhibits are already in as exhibits because they were admitted via 92 bis. We, of course, are not opposed now to removing those because they were admitted into evidence on the condition that he would come to appear as a witness and be cross-examined. Since that's not going to happen, we, of course, have no opposition to dropping those from the -- those exhibits out and removing them. So I just wanted to inform the Court of that and also Defence counsel because he -- he may -- I don't know, but he may have been reached tomorrow. So I wanted to let the Court know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What may have happened tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We may have reached him tomorrow. I'm not sure how long the cross-examination of this witness will go, but that's why I wanted to tell the Court today that we're dropping him and we'll move to the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry that -- if we could redact that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I -- the next witness I do not believe will be available tomorrow, unfortunately; he will only be available on Thursday. So if this cross-examination finishes early, then we will have a short gap tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How long are you going to you be, Mr. Milovancevic with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, two sessions would be realistic, but with respect to the previous witness, the Great Gatsby, we of course agree that he be left out of the list with one condition, that his testimony be withdrawn from the files.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Naturally that would happen, Mr. Milovancevic. When you say two sessions, you mean two more sessions from now on that you still want to spend with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that is my assessment, although I'm proceeding far faster than I expected to do. But I'm just being cautious. Out of an abundance of caution, not to overstep the deadline. That is what I think, two sittings after this, and depending on the lieutenant colonel's answers, we might be more efficient. We'll try to go through as soon as possible of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, then, Mr. Milovancevic. And, Mr. Whiting, you will -- we will deal with what you were talking about a little later, maybe early next session, the question of whether or not you want to withdraw this witness and his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm -- okay. But I'm -- I'm not clear, Your Honour. Is there an issue about this or -- about whether we can drop him as a witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There is an issue, yes. Yeah, there is an issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Is it possible -- would it be possible to address it now because we would otherwise send the witness home if he's not going to be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Judge Nosworthy wants to present an issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, I do have an issue as a matter of procedure. My understanding of 92 bis would be that the evidence in chief is technically already in, and my question, therefore, would be, could you withdraw it at this point in time as opposed to allowing it to remain on the record as part of the record under 92 bis and to make the witness available for cross-examination by the Defence if the Defence so chooses? So on a procedural point, I would ask you to address me and the Chamber concerning which is the correct course to adopt.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I understand Your Honour's question. The -- the evidence was admitted by the Court's decision via Rule 92 bis on the condition that the witness come for cross-examination. Ordinarily what happens when that happens is that the witness appears, and at the moment the witness appears then the evidence is put into evidence 92 bis, the evidence in chief, and the witness is cross-examined. We -- we worked a little bit more efficient and we provided the evidence to the Chamber and the exhibits so they were already given assigned exhibit numbers. However, I think that until the witness actually appears, it still -- the witness is still within the control of the Prosecution. It's still the Prosecution's witness, and it's still within the Prosecution's power to decide whether the witness will be called or not and, therefore, I would submit that the witness -- we can still pull the witness from the witness list at this time. If the Chamber has a different understanding, we would move then to withdraw his evidence. I don't think -- from what I hear from Defence counsel, they concur with having him withdrawn, and therefore I think that that would be the most expeditious solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: That is the material statement I was looking for, Mr. Whiting. You have put it in perspective now that we have heard that the Defence is concurring in your application, but I was concerned about removing the right of cross-examination by virtue of the course that you attempted to -- were attempting to adopt, which I believe would have been provided for the Defence. But now you have explained it in the proper perspective, then my concern would have dissipated. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Then we will proceed, then, Your Honour, that we will not be calling that witness. He will be withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: If the Defence is ad idem, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Defence is ad idem, isn't it? "Yes," will suffice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I accept what my learned colleague of the Prosecution has just said. All I wanted to ask is to clarify the question of the statement already. So now we hear that the Prosecutor is withdrawing everything, witness and all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then you need no order, you're just going to withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Your Honour. I think it's sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Court adjourned. Tomorrow, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 7th day of June, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.
